name: nmap
desc: Network scanner — discover hosts, open ports, services, and OS versions. The Swiss Army knife of network recon.

usage.cmt: ping sweep — discover live hosts, no port scan
aggressive scan: OS, version, scripts, traceroute
all 65535 ports, show only open ones
UDP scan for DNS and SNMP

quick_flags.desc: ping sweep only — no port scan
save output in all formats simultaneously

scenarios: Auditing which ports are exposed on a server before going to production
Discovering all devices on a network segment
Verifying a firewall rule change actually blocked the intended port

mistakes.x: Running nmap -A on production without permission — intrusive
mistakes.fix: Use -sn (ping sweep) or -sV (version) for less intrusive scans; full -A generates significant traffic and logs
Use -oA filename to save in all formats (normal, XML, grepable) simultaneously

secnote: nmap is dual-use. Defenders use it for asset inventory and vulnerability assessment. Attackers use it for recon. Unauthorized nmap scanning is illegal in many jurisdictions. Always have written permission.
tags: nmap scan port host network discover recon audit security

name: dig
desc: DNS lookup and diagnostics. More powerful than nslookup with cleaner output.

usage.cmt: trace full delegation path from root servers

quick_flags.desc: trace full delegation from root servers
record type: A, MX, TXT, CNAME, NS, PTR

scenarios: DNS change not propagating — query multiple resolvers to check
Email delivery issues — check MX records and SPF/DKIM
Investigating DNS hijacking — compare results from different resolvers

mistakes.fix: dig gives TTL, authoritative flags, full section breakdown. nslookup is legacy and inconsistent

mistakes.x: Not using +trace to diagnose delegation issues
mistakes.fix: dig +trace walks the full delegation chain and shows exactly where the problem is in DNS hierarchy

tags: dns lookup record query mx a ptr cname ttl nameserver

name: nslookup
desc: Query DNS servers interactively or non-interactively. Available on both Linux and Windows.

quick_flags.desc: specify record type: A, MX, TXT, NS, PTR
second argument: use this DNS server instead of default

scenarios: Quick DNS check on Windows where dig is not installed
Checking if SPF records are published correctly for email
Verifying a newly deployed domain is resolving

mistakes.x: nslookup uses system resolver by default — may return cached results
mistakes.fix: Always specify a server: nslookup example.com 8.8.8.8 to bypass local cache

mistakes.x: Not specifying record type gets only A record
mistakes.fix: Use -type=MX, -type=TXT etc. for other record types

tags: nslookup dns windows linux lookup query name resolution

name: tshark (Wireshark CLI)
desc: Command-line version of Wireshark. Capture and analyze packets without a GUI.
scenarios: Headless server — capture packets without GUI
Automated packet capture in scripts
Filtering a large pcap for specific protocol or IP before opening in Wireshark

mistakes.x: Not specifying -c or a time limit — runs until disk is full
mistakes.fix: Always use -c COUNT or -a duration:SECONDS to limit capture size

mistakes.x: Capturing without saving — lose the data
mistakes.fix: Add -w output.pcap for any serious capture that will need later analysis

secnote: tshark can extract plaintext credentials from unencrypted protocols. This is a critical tool for both network forensics and for understanding why your protocols MUST use TLS.
tags: tshark wireshark packet capture network analysis pcap protocol

name: arp
desc: View and manipulate the ARP cache — maps IP addresses to MAC addresses.

usage.cmt: display full ARP table (works on Linux and Windows)
delete a specific ARP entry (force refresh)
modern Linux equivalent with more detail

quick_flags.desc: delete ARP cache entry for IP

scenarios: Two devices claiming same IP — check ARP table for duplicate MACs
After router replacement — ARP cache pointing to old MAC
Investigating ARP spoofing/poisoning attack

mistakes.x: ARP cache entries expire — a clean table may just mean no recent traffic
mistakes.fix: Ping the target first to populate the cache, then run arp -a
For ARP spoofing defense, use static entries arp -s for critical hosts (gateway, DNS)

secnote: ARP spoofing (poisoning) is a classic MitM attack. If two different MACs claim the same IP in your ARP table — especially the gateway IP — you may have an active ARP attack. Check with: arp -a | grep GATEWAY_IP.
tags: arp mac address ip table cache spoofing mitm network layer2

name: route / ip route
desc: View and manage the IP routing table. Determine where packets will be sent.

usage.cmt: show which interface and gateway would be used for a specific destination

quick_flags.desc: show which route would be used for destination
delete all routes (danger: drops all connectivity)

scenarios: After VPN connects but traffic still goes direct — routing table wrong
Server can reach local network but not internet — missing default route
Split-tunnel VPN not routing corporate subnets correctly

mistakes.x: route add on Linux (old command) changes not persistent across reboots
mistakes.fix: For persistent routes, add to /etc/network/interfaces or use nmcli
Use ip route get DESTINATION to verify which route is actually selected

tags: routing table route ip gateway default network path forwarding

name: iperf3
desc: Measure network bandwidth between two hosts. Requires iperf3 on both ends.

usage.cmt: start iperf3 in server mode (on the target machine)
run bandwidth test to server (client side)

quick_flags.desc: run as client connecting to HOST

scenarios: Network feels slow — measure actual throughput vs expected bandwidth
After cabling or switch change — verify full speed is achievable
Testing Wi-Fi vs wired performance difference

mistakes.x: Running iperf3 test over production traffic path during business hours
mistakes.fix: Schedule bandwidth tests during maintenance windows — a 30s iperf3 test saturates the link

mistakes.x: Single-stream test not representative of real-world throughput
mistakes.fix: Use -P 4 for parallel streams to better simulate actual multi-connection workloads

tags: bandwidth speed throughput network test iperf performance measurement

name: ufw (firewall)
desc: Uncomplicated Firewall — simplified iptables management for Ubuntu/Debian systems.

usage.cmd: ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/8 to any port 3306
usage.cmt: allow MySQL from internal network only
activate firewall (ensure SSH is allowed first!)

quick_flags.desc: show rules, default policies, and active status
block all traffic from an IP
remove a rule by number (get numbers via status numbered)
disable ufw and delete all rules

scenarios: New server setup — enable firewall with minimum exposure
Block an IP after detecting brute force
Open a port for a new application only from specific network

mistakes.x: ufw enable before allowing SSH — locks you out
ufw deny blocks new connections but doesn't kill existing ones
mistakes.fix: To immediately drop active connections from a host, use iptables -I INPUT 1 -s IP -j DROP

secnote: Proper rule order matters: ufw processes rules top-to-bottom, first match wins. Use ufw insert NUMBER for priority. A deny-all default with explicit allows is better than allow-all with explicit denies.
tags: ufw firewall rules allow deny block port ip ubuntu linux
